passage: Tutor's note, Thursday. Yamini's classmates did an imitation of her accent in the corridor today, and one of them, Vaibhav, held his nose at her home-cooked lunch and said, "just banter, yaar." Yamini laughed along, but her eyes went to the floor and she wrapped her tiffin in her bag quickly. At the end of the day I asked her to stay back. She said, "I laugh so they don't think I'm sensitive. But it hurts." I told her the mockery was not hers to carry. She practised a plain sentence with me: "That's not okay with me." Yamini said it to Vaibhav on Friday morning, and he went quiet, then said sorry. I have spoken to the whole class about mimicry. I will check in with her next week.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do at Yamini's lunch?
qa.a: Vaibhav held his nose at her home-cooked lunch and called it just banter.

qa.q: Why did Yamini laugh along with the mimicking?
qa.a: She laughed so people would not think she was sensitive, though it hurt her.

qa.q: What plain sentence helped Yamini respond?
qa.a: She practised the sentence "That's not okay with me" and said it to Vaibhav.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav have seen the mimicry before Yamini spoke up?
qa.a: As harmless banter, since Yamini laughed along, though her reply made him go quiet and apologise.

grounding: Classmates mimic her accent and food and call it banter; she laughs along while hurt, then tells them plainly it is not fine.
